SC101
Diabetes aggravates heat stroke induced blood-brain
barrier breakdown, oedema formation and brain
pathology
D.F. Muresanu
1, A. Sharma2, H.S. Sharma2
1DepartmentofNeurology,UniversityofMedicineandPharmacy
“IuliuHatieganu”,Cluj-Napoca,Romania,2DepartmentofSurgical
Sciences,AnaesthesiologyandIntensiveCareMedicine,University
Hospital,UppsalaUniversity,Uppsala,Sweden
The incidences of heat stroke associated with heat stress have
increased during summer months among European populations due
to global warming. However, this is still unclear whether popula-
tions suffering from disorders of endocrine metabolism, e.g., dia-
betes mellitus is equally or more sensitive to heat stroke induced
pathophysiology. Since chronic renal hypertension exacerbates the
blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, brain oedema formation and
cell injury in a rat model of heat stroke, the present investigation
was aimed at understanding the brain pathophysiology of hyperther-
mia in an experimental diabetic rat model. Rats were treated with
streptozotocine once daily for 3 days (50 mg/kg, i.p.) and allowed to
survive 4 weeks to reach a blood glucose level between 18 and 20
mMol/l). Control rats received saline in identical manner (blood
glucose 4–6 mMol/l). Both control and diabetic rats were subjected
to 4 h heat stress at 38° C in a biological oxygen demand incubator
(BOD). This experimental condition induces profound disruption of
the BBB to Evans blue and radioiodine and results in massive brain
oedema formation and cell injury. Subjection of diabetic rats to 4 h
at 38° C resulted in exacerbation of hyperthermia (>41.4° C), BBB
disruption, brain oedema formation and brain pathology compared
to the control group. The most marked cell damage in the diabetic
rats was seen in the brain stem reticular information and in the
cerebellum followed by hippocampus and cortex. These observa-
tions suggest that diabetes population is highly vulnerable to heat
stress induced brain pathology, not reported earlier.
SC102
Decreased insulin sensitivity and dyslipidemia are
strongly associated with ischemic stroke and asym-
ptomatic carotid artery stenosis in non-diabetics
M. Mijajlovic
1, A. Jotic2, N. Lalic2, A. Pavlovic1,
J. Zidverc-Trajkovic1, Z. Jovanovic1, N. Sternic1
1InstituteofNeurology,2InstituteofEndocrinology,ClinicalCentre
ofSerbia,Belgrade,Serbia
Background and aims: Decreased insulin sensitivity (IS) with
compensatory hyperinsulinemia plays a crucial role in the patho-
genesis of atherosclerosis, but its role in ischemic stroke (IST) has
not yet been elucidated. This study was aimed at analyzing IS as
the indicator of atherosclerotic activity, as well as plasma insulin
(PI) levels and dyslipidemia pattern in 100 patients with
atherothrombotic IST confirmed in brain computerized tomogra-
phy/magnetic resonance imaging – (group A); 100 patients with
asymptomatic stenosis of one or both internal carotid arteries
/H1135050% – (group B), and 50 healthy controls – (group C). Patients
with diabetes mellitus and ischemic heart disease were excluded
from the study.
Material and methods: IS was determined by Homeostasis
Assessment Model (HOMA-IR), PI levels were determined by
radioimmunoassay. We measured total cholesterol, LDL and HDL
cholesterol and trygliceride levels in all groups.
Results: IS was significantly lower in group A compared to group
B and C (3.82±0.27 vs. 2.69±0.22, p<0.05; 3.82±0.27 vs.

1.51±0.22, p<0.01). PI levels were significantly higher in group A
in comparison to group B and C (16.00±1.2 vs. 11.95±0.88,
p<0.05; 16.00±1.2 vs. 7.12±0.19, p<0.01). Different patterns of
dyslipidemia were observed in ACAS in comparison to IST.
Conclusion: Our results indicate that atherothrombotic IST as well
as ACAS are strongly associated with decreased IS and increased
PI levels, although all the patients were non diabetics. Also, differ-
ent patterns of dyslipidemia between ACAS and IST were
observed.
SC103
Sub-cutaneous insulin for blood-glucose reduction in
acute ischaemic stroke
N. Siafarikas
1,6, C. Moebius2, M. Amador3, C. Beyer1,
N. Janssen-Rosseck4, C. Stapf 3, J.P. Mohr5, H. Mast6
1DepartmentofNeurology,Bergmannstrost,Halle,2Departmentof
Neurology,UniversityofErlangen,Germany,3Departmentof
Neurology,Lariboisiere,Paris,France,4DepartmentofNeurology,
UniversitätDresden,Germany,5DepartmentofNeurology,Columbia
University,NewYork,NY,USA,6DepartmentofStrokeMedicine,
UniversityofNottingham,UK
Background: Elevated blood-glucose is associated with a worse
outcome of ischaemic stroke. A prior study investigating the effect
of intravenous insulin on stroke-outcome achieved only a modest
glucose-reduction, included mostly patients with stroke-onset
beyond 12 hours and showed no beneficial clinical effect. We test-
ed the use of sub-cutaneous insulin within the first 12 hours after
stroke-onset.
Methods: The safety, feasibility, and proof of concept observation-
al pilot-study included 30 consecutive acute stroke-patients (mean
age 64 years, 37% female, <12 hours after stroke onset). Targeting
normal-range blood-glucose of 4 to 6 mmol/l hyperglycaemic
patients (n=12) were treated using sub-cutaneous insulin (from 4
units for patients with blood glucose values of 6 to 8 mmol/l to 16
units for glucose values 18 to 20 mmol/l). The 18 normoglycaemic
patients served as controls.
Results: At 3 hours after start of treatment the baseline mean
blood-glucose of hyperglycaemic patients had fallen from 8.3 to
5.5 mmol/l (p<0.05) with 9 out of 12 patients reaching the target-
range. At 6 and 24 hours the mean glucose-values in the hypergly-
caemic group (4.6 and 6.0 mmol/l) were still within target-range,
with no significant difference to controls (4.5 and 5.5 mmol/l). No
patient developed clinical or laboratory signs of hypoglycaemia or

SC104
Exacerbation of stroke symptoms by infection and
metabolic perturbations - a diffusion-weighted MRI
study
S.J. Iyadurai
1, K.L. Knievel2, M.S. Flaster1
1DepartmentofNeurology,BarrowNeurologicalInstitute,
2DepartmentofInternalMedicine,St.Joseph’sHospitalandMedical
Center,Phoenix,AZ,USA
Background: Acute ischemia secondary to a thromboembolic
event is the most common cause of stroke in adults. It is important
to distinguish new ischemia from exacerbation of prior ischemic
deficits. Conventional teaching has emphasized that acute exacer-
bations of prior neurological deficits may happen in conjunction
with acute microbial infection or metabolic derangement. How-
ever, there is no study that has actually demonstrated this fact. To
date, Diffusion-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (DW-MRI)
remains the most sensitive and specific marker for new ischemia.
Design and methods: Case Series.
Results: Our initial analysis included patients with history of pre-
vious strokes, who presented with acute-onset of worsening of
their prior neurological deficits (n=33), DW-MRI was performed
on 27 patients. DW-MRI analysis in most instances (n=15) did not
reveal any new strokes. In these patients, infection or metabolic
abnormality was concurrently noted.
Conclusions and relevance: It is commonly believed that sys-
temic infections exacerbate “old” stroke symptoms. Our study bol-
sters such an idea with evidence from DW-MRI. A history of past
strokes and a concurrent infection most likely identify a state
where old symptoms are exacerbated by infection rather than a new
stroke event. A larger study of this kind may yield predictive fea-
tures that would help an emergency room physician or stroke neu-
rologist distinguish new ischemia from simple worsening where
emergent DWI is not available and prompt appropriate treatment.
SC105
Carotid arteriosclerotic plaque morphology may pre-
dict the intracerebral ischemic lesion load: a 3 Tesla
MRI study
M.L. Mono
1, A. Galimanis1, M. El Koussy2, M. Arnold1,
J. Gralla2, H.P. Mattle1, G. Schroth2, K. Nedeltchev1
1DepartmentofNeurology,2DepartmentofNeuroradiology,
Inselspital,BernUniversityHospitalandUniversityofBern,
Switzerland
Background: Carotid arteriosclerosis is a major cause of stroke.
Traditionally, the degree of stenosis has been used to assess the risk
of thromboembolism originating from an arteriosclerotic plaque
(AP). Recent data suggest that histological composition of the AP
might also be related to the risk of stroke.
Aim: To determine the association between AP morphology and
the cerebral ischemic lesion load in the territory of the correspon-
ding internal carotid artery (ICA).
Patients and methods:10 patients (mean age 67 years) underwent
a 3 Tesla MRI of the carotid bifurcation and the brain. The follow-
ing plaque morphology features were correlated with the number
of ischemic lesions in the corresponding brain territory:
intraplaque haemorrhage, thin/disrupted fibrous cap, large lipid
core.
Results: 4 patients had a stenosis of the right ICA, 5 had a steno-
sis of the left ICA, and 1 had non-stenotic APs in both carotid

arteries. There were 4 high grade, 1 moderate and 4 lower grade
ICA stenoses. Stenoses were symptomatic in 3 patients and asymp-
tomatic in 7 patients. 4 of the 7 patients with asymptomatic
stenoses had silent ischemic lesions on brain MRI. There was a
weak correlation between the presence of a large lipid core and the
ischemic lesion load in the corresponding brain territory (r=0.266).
Neither the degree of stenosis, nor the presence of thin/disrupted
fibrous cap or intraplaque haemorrhage were correlated to the
intracerebral ischemic lesion load.
Conclusions: These results suggest that the presence of a large
lipid core may help identifying vulnerable arteriosclerotic plaques.

SC107
Phenotype of patients responsive to sub-occipital
neurostimulation for refractory head pain
K. Paemeleire
1, J.P. Van Buyten2, M. Van Buynder2, D. Alicino2,
G. Van Maele3, I. Smet2, P .J. Goadsby4
1DepartmentofNeurology,GhentUniversityHospital,Ghent,
2PainClinic,AZNikolaas,Sint-Niklaas,3DepartmentofMedical
InformaticsandStatistics,GhentUniversityHospital,Ghent,
Belgium,4HeadacheGroup,DepartmentofNeurology,University
ofCaliforniaSanFrancisco,CA,USA
Objective: Sub-occipital nerve stimulation (ONS) has been
employed off-label for medically refractory head pain. Identifica-
tion of specific headache diagnoses responding to this modality of
treatment is required.
Methods: 44 patients with medically refractory head pain treated
with ONS at a Pain Clinic were invited for a clinical interview and,
if necessary, an indomethacin test, to establish the headache pheno-
type according to the International Classification of Headache Dis-
orders Second Edition (ICHD-II). We gathered data from question-
naires before implantation, at one month after implantation, and –
if available – at long-term follow-up.
Results:26 patients gave informed consent. At one month follow-up
and at long-term follow-up a significant decrease in all pain vari-
ables was noted, as well as in analgesic use. Quality of sleep and
quality of life improved. Patient satisfaction was generally high, as
80% of patients had at least 50% pain relief at long-term follow-up.
The overall complication rate was low, but revisions were frequent.
After phenotyping two main groups emerged: eight patients had
“Migraine without aura” (ICHD-II 1.1) and eight patients had “Con-
stant pain caused by compression, irritation or distortion of cranial
nerves or upper cervical roots by structural lesions” (ICHD-II
13.12). Overuse of acute headache treatments was associated with
less favourable long-term outcome in migraine patients.
Conclusion: Careful clinical phenotyping may help in defining
subgroups that are more likely to respond to ONS for refractory
headache. Migraine patients particularly should be monitored for
medication overuse. A controlled prospective study for ONS in
ICHD-II 13.12 is warranted.

SC108
Long-term depression of pain-related cerebral activa-
tion in healthy men: an fMRI study
S. Rottmann
1, K. Jung2, J. Ellrich2
1ICCRBIOMAT,MedicalFaculty,RWTHAachenUniversity,
Aachen,Germany,2SMI,DepartmentofHealthScienceand
Technology,MedicalFaculty,AalborgUniversity,Aalborg,Denmark
Electrical low-frequency stimulation (LFS) of cutaneous afferents
reliably induces long-term depression (LTD) of spinal nociception
and pain in man. Aim of this study was the investigation of LFS
effects on cerebral activation by functional magnetic resonance
imaging (fMRI). In 12 healthy male volunteers (20 to 28 years)
nociceptive A/H9254fibres of right hand dorsum were electrically stim-
ulated by a concentric electrode. Test stimulation series [3x5 stim-
uli at 0.33 Hz (stimulation period) with 15 seconds interval each
(rest period)] and LFS (1 Hz, 1200 pulses) were applied with inten-
sities of 4-fold pain threshold. Two test stimulation series each
were performed before and after LFS or no stimulation period
(Control). V olunteers rated sensory and affective pain perception.
Significance level of fMRI data was set to p<0.001 uncorrected.
Before LFS, contrast between stimulation and rest period showed
activation in pain related brain areas, including primary (S1) and
secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) and insula. After LFS, con-
trast between stimulation and rest period revealed no significance.
Contrast between stimulation periods before and after LFS indicat-
ed reduced activation in S1 and anterior cingulate gyrus (ACC)
after LFS. Sensory and affective pain ratings decreased after LFS.
In a control experiment, no differences in fMRI data and ratings
were observed. This fMRI study revealed activation in brain areas
involved in sensory (S1, S2) and affective (insula) pain processing.
After LFS, cerebral activity decreased (sensory: S1, affective:
ACC). Ratings confirm reductions in sensory and affective compo-
nents of pain after LFS. LFS induces sustained depression in cere-
bral activity and pain perception.
SC109
Spinal cord stimulation versus conventional medical
management for failed back surgery syndrome: long-
term results from the PROCESS study
M. Meglio
, B. Cioni, S. Sabene
DepartmentofFunctionalandSpinalNeurosurgery,Gemelli
CatholicUniversityHospital,Rome,Italy
Background and aims: Patients with failed back surgery syn-
drome (FBSS) experience chronic pain, disability, and reduced
health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Few pain studies report
long-term treatment results. PROCESS investigates the 24-months
effectiveness of the addition of spinal cord stimulation (SCS) to
conventional medical management (CMM) in FBSS patients.
Methods: The PROCESS trial randomized 100 FBSS patients
with predominant radicular leg pain to SCS (n=52) plus CMM or
CMM alone (n=48). Primary objective: /H1135050% leg pain relief at
6 months (V AS). Secondary outcomes: HRQoL (SF-36), function
(Oswestry), patient satisfaction, and complications. At 6 months,
SCS patients reported better pain relief, HRQoL and function
(p<0.05 for all comparisons) than CMM patients. Cross-over
(allowed after 6 months) was requested by 32 (73%) CMM versus
5 (10%) SCS patients. We report outcomes of SCS treatment in
patients randomized to SCS continuing stimulation at 24 months.
We also compared the primary outcome between SCS and CMM
based on the final treatment received.

Results: At 24 months, the group of 42 patients randomized to
SCS who continued SCS reported significant improvement in leg
pain (p<0.0001), HRQoL (p/H113490.01 for 7/8 SF-36 domains), and
function (p=0.0002) compared with baseline. 13 patients (31%)
experienced device-related complications requiring surgical proce-
dure. In a “final treatment received” analysis, 1/15 (7%) patients
receiving CMM at 24 months achieved/H1135050% leg pain relief, com-
pared to 34/72 (47%) patients on SCS (p=0.02).
Conclusions: In selected FBSS patients, SCS provides sustained
leg pain relief with lasting and important improvements in health-
related quality of life, functional capacity, and patient satisfaction.
SC110
Modulation of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)
through repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
(rTMS) during capsaicin induced pain: effects on
nociceptive control and motor cortical circuits
F. Giglia
1, M. De Tommaso2, F. Brighina1, A. Palermo1,
M.L. Panetta1, A. Puma1, G. Cosentino1, G. Giglia1, B. Fierro1
1DepartmentofClinicalNeurosciences,UniversityofPalermo,
2DepartmentofNeurosciencesandPsychiatry,UniversityofBari,
Italy
Objective: To study the effect of DLPFC activation (through
rTMS) on nociceptive control in a model of capsaicine-induced
pain, exploring also the modulatory effects of capsaicine and
rTMS on intracortical motor circuits.
Methods: We studied in healthy subjects pain responses to cap-
saicine applied on right or left hand, in four separate experiments:
1: in 10 subjects, pain responses to capsaicine were evaluated in
baseline and after 5 Hz rTMS over left DLPFC, at 10 (5 subjects)
or 20 minutes (5 subjects) after capsaicine, in separate sessions. 2:
In 8 subjects, rTMS was given over right DLPFC following the
same paradigm. 3: sham (ineffective) rTMS was used in 5 subjects.
4: capsaicine and DLPFC rTMS effects on motor cortex (5 more
subjects) were evaluated through cortico-spinal excitability (test-
MEP), intracortical inhibition (ICI) and facilitation (ICF) by
paired-pulse TMS. These parameters were measured in baseline
and after capsaicine with and without rTMS. In experiments 3 and
4 rTMS was given over left DLPFC, as right-DLPFC-rTMS
(experiment 2) showed no effect on pain measures.
Results: Left-DLPFC-rTMS significantly decreases capsaicine-
induced pain in both hands. No significant effect on pain-measures
was observed after right-DLPFC or sham-rTMS. Capsaicine
affected motor cortical excitability significantly reducing test MEP
amplitude, decreasing ICI (only at 30 min after application) and
increasing ICF for a longer time (from 20-40 min after applica-
tion). Left DLPFC rTMS (10 min after capsaicine) was able to
revert capsaicine effects.
Conclusions: Left DLPFC seems to exert a bilateral control on
pain system modulating also the effects on motor intracortical cir-
cuits. Left DLPFC could therefore represent an alternative target
for pain treatment protocols

Evaluation of lacosamide in diabetic neuropathic pain
trials

1, S. Bongardt2, K. Sommerville3

the efficacy and safety of the investigational antinociceptive and

in average daily pain score (11-point pain scale) from baseline to

baseline to the end of maintenance for the flexible-dose trial. Sub-
jects receiving lacosamide 400 mg/day (n=426) showed numerical-

400 mg/day significantly reduced pain and showed good tolerabil-
ity in clinical trials of DNP .

Intracarotid administration improves the closed cranial
window model in rats, a preclinical migraine model, by
enhancing the accuracy and circumventing the
systemic effects
S. Gupta
, L.J. Boni, J. Olesen
DepartmentofNeurology,GlostrupUniversityHospital,Glostrup,
Denmark
Background and aims: Intravital microscopy on closed cranial
window in rats has been extensively utilized in migraine research
with a credible predicative value, in which increase in diameter of
cranial blood vessels after intravenous administration is measured.
Number of putative targets being studied in migraine research is
large peptide molecules such as calcitonin gene-related peptide
(CGRP), pituitary adenylate cyclase activating poly peptide-38
(P ACAP-38) and adrenomedullin. These peptides are metabolised
rapidly and thus higher doses of these peptides have to be admin-
istered. Not only higher doses involve higher cost but also have
systemic effect such as drop in blood pressure which also influ-
ences the cranial blood vessel diameter by auto regulation.
Methods: In this study we used an in-dwelling catheter in carotid
artery and studied the responses in dural artery in male rats. We
used CGRP , PACAP-38, adrenomedullin and capsaicin for the
study and compared the dose response curve when administered
intravenously vs. intracarotid.
Results: Administration of CGRP , PACAP-38 and intracarotid
capsaicin increased the potency by 9, 26 and 20 fold respectively,
with minimal decrease in blood pressure compared to intravenous
infusion. BIBN4096BS, a CGRP antagonist, potency is increased
by 13 times on intracarotid administration. We also topically
applied CGRP , which showed a dose dependent increase in dural
artery diameter.
Conclusions: Therefore, this approach offers an improvement over
the existing model of closed cranial window by circumventing sig-
nificant systemic effects and thus providing more accurate read out

of effect of these agents on the dural vasculature pivotal in
migraine pathogenesis.

Non-manipulative unilateral proximal arm automatisms
lateralize contralaterally in temporal lobe epilepsy
A. Kelemen
1, A. Fogarasi1, J. Janszky2, P. Halasz1
1NationalInstituteofNeurosurgery,Budapest,2NeurologyClinic,
UniversityofPecs,Hungary
Background and aims: Hand automatisms are considered to be
ipsilateral seizure lateralizing sign in temporal lobe epilepsy
(TLE). We describe different types of contralateral upper extremi-
ty automatisms (CUEA).
Methods: 193 video-EEG recordings of 55 patients with
favourable postoperative outcome (Engel 1,2) after standardized
temporal lobectomy were reviewed. 57 seizures of 21 patients were
selected with contralateral upper extremity automatisms. We eval-
uated their electroclinical characteristics and relation to other later-
alizing motor symptoms.
Results: T wo types of CUEAs were observed. Manipulative/distal
type of CUEAs occurred in 11 seizures of 7 patients unilaterally,
and in 32 seizures of 14 patients bilaterally. They were seen in all
phases of the seizures including the postictal state. Non-manipula-
tive, proximal arm automatisms were seen exclusively unilaterally
and always contralaterally to the operated side. These automatisms
were always rhythmic and had some circulatory component resem-
bling arm or forearm waving / flaunting / circling or stirring move-
ments. They occurred in 29 seizures (15%) of 12 (21%) of patients,
in most seizures in the first third, and never post-ictally, in various
time sequences combined with dystonic/tonic posturing or limb
immobility (in 9 seizures before; in 8 after; in 9 mixed). This high-
ly lateralized type of automatism was seen in cases irrespective of
etiology.
Conclusions: Non-manipulative unilateral proximal arm automa-
tism is a reliable lateralizing sign (to the contralateral hemisphere)
in TLE. This sign may be pathophysiologically related to dyston-
ic/tonic posturing. Manipulative distal automatisms have less later-
alizing value.

Fast oscillations during interictal spikes localize the
epileptogenic zone in patients with partial epilepsy
A.G. Guggisberg
1,2, H.E. Kirsch2,3, M.M. Mantle2, N.M. Barbaro4,
S.S. Nagarajan2
1DepartmentofClinicalNeurosciences,UniversityHopital,Geneva,
Switzerland,2BiomagneticImagingLaboratory,3Departmentof
Neurology,4DepartmentofNeurologicalSurgery,UCSF,San
Francisco,CA,USA
Background: Interictal epileptic spikes are defined as fast tran-
sients. Reconstructing the sources of high-frequency activity there-
fore might be a promising approach for localizing epileptogenic
tissue. In this study, we tested the usefulness of maps of spike-
locked power increases in the beta and gamma band for determin-
ing the epileptogenic zone in a population of 27 consecutive
presurgical patients with medication refractory partial epilepsies.
Methods: Resting state magnetoencephalography (MEG) was co-
registered with high-resolution structural MRI. Interictal epileptic
spikes were manually marked and the sources of spike-locked
power increases in the beta and gamma bands were localized using
an adaptive spatial filtering method. As gold standard for deter-
mining the correct location of the epileptogenic zone, we used the
location of surgically resected tissue in patients with good post-sur-

Results: In patients with good surgical outcome after a mean fol-

The spectrum and clinical features of patients with
malformations of cortical development and epilepsy
G. Kuchukhidze
1, I. Unterberger1, J. Dobesberger1, G. Walser1,
E. Haberlandt2, F. Koppelstaetter3, T. Gotwald3, M. Ortler4,
S. Felber3, E. Trinka1
1DepartmentofNeurology,2DepartmentofPediatrics,3Department
ofRadiologyII,4DepartmentofNeurosurgery,MedicalUniversityof
Innsbruck,Austria
Background and aims: Malformations of cortical development
(MCD) are increasingly recognised as a major cause for pharma-
coresistant seizures, neurological deficits and cognitive distur-
bances. This study aimed at identifying spectrum and clinical fea-
tures of patients with MCD and epilepsy.
Methods: We identified 237 patients (127w/110m) aged 1-75
years (mean 31.19 years) with MCD and epilepsy at the Seizure

Background and aims:Behavioural studies report semantic prim-
ing effects as faster responses to target words preceded by seman-
tically related primes in comparison to semantically unrelated
ones. In bilinguals, this effect is observed together with a language
effect, which is faster in responses to targets in the first (L1) than
in the second (L2) language. Here, we investigated the event-relat-
ed potential (ERPs) correlates of the semantic and language effects
in bilinguals
Methods: ERPs were collected from right-handed bilinguals dur-
ing a semantic categorisation task. Subjects were presented with
word pairs in same or different languages and decided whether
words in each pair were semantically related or not.
Results: Reaction times showed significant language (p<0.001)
and semantic relation effects (p<0.0001). Electrophysiologically,
the relation effect differentiated ERPs at 400 ms (N400 compo-
nent). Earlier on, a map segment appearing ~180 ms was longer in
L2 than in L1 conditions (p<0.01). Source localisation showed that
the first segment activated the left fusiform gyrus and occipital
areas bilaterally while the N400-related response recruited addi-
tionally the middle/superior temporal cortex bilaterally.
Conclusion: Our analysis allowed dissociating language and

semantic relation effects in time and space. Reading in L1 and L2
appears to differ early during word recognition processes involving
the fusiform gyrus. Semantic analysis of words, not differing
between languages, supports the view of a common conceptual
representation (SNF no’ grant 325100-118362).

Background:Perfusion weighted magnet resonance imaging (PW-
MRI) based maps of cerebral blood flow (mriCBF) are seldom
used in clinical routine. We aimed at defining the performance of
mriCBF by comparison with quantitative CBF measurement using
15O-water positron emission tomography (petCBF).
Methods: In acute stroke patients, comparative CBF measurement
by PET and MRI was performed. Post-processing included the use
of an arterial input function. Several mriCBF thresholds
(<40,<30,<20,<10 ml/100 g/min) were applied and the best match
to the hypoperfusion ,<20 ml/100 g/min on PET was identified.
The resulting degree of congruence was expressed as the ratio C
(C= V olume mriCBF / V olume petCBF). A region of interest
placed in the unaffected hemisphere was used for an additional
individual normalisation.
Results: In 24 stroke patients (median time MRI to PET: 68 min-
utes; 16 patients imaged within 24 hours after stroke) the median
volume of penumbral flow (petCBF) was 78.5 ccm. On visual
inspection, an excellent qualitative congruence was found for
mriCBF . In the pooled analysis, mriCBF <20 ml/100 g/min best
identified penumbral flow (median C-ratio: 1.0) but showed a wide
interindividual range (C-ratio: 0.3 to 3.5). The additional normali-
sation significantly improved the performance of MRI imaging
(range of C-ratio: 0.7 to 1.8).
Discussion: CBF maps using a threshold of <20 ml/100 g/min
well identified penumbral flow. However, a considerable interindi-
vidual variance was found even with the use of an AIF algorhythm.
This variance was markedly improved by a simple additional cor-
rection factor. Our results underline the need for a further specifi-
cation of the MRI based perfusion assessment.

Background: Functional maps of eloquent brain regions are
increasingly used during surgical planning in patients with brain
lesions, but their accuracy can depend on patient cooperation and
on study paradigms that are capable of reliably activating the brain
area of interest. We propose to map non-functional, necrotic or
structurally disconnected brain areas according to their decreased
functional connectivity with intact regions.
Methods: Magnetoencephalographic (MEG) recordings of corti-
cal activity were obtained from 15 consecutive patients with focal
brain lesions and from 14 healthy controls during resting state.
Neural activity in the brain was reconstructed using an adaptive

spatial filtering technique. The imaginary component of the com-
plex valued coherence was calculated for pairs of brain voxels and
used as an index of their functional connectivity.

Results: The alpha frequency range corresponding to the human
cortical idling rhythm showed the greatest imaginary coherence
magnitude in all subjects. In healthy subjects, eloquent brain areas
had greater alpha coherence than non-critical areas. When com-
pared to healthy controls, all patients with focal brain lesions had
diffuse or scattered brain areas with decreased alpha coherence.
Patients with lesion-induced neurological deficits displayed
decreased connectivity estimates in the corresponding brain area
compared to intact contralateral regions. In patients with tumours
who did not have preoperative neurological deficits, brain areas
showing low coherence could be surgically resected without the
occurrence of postoperative deficits.
Conclusion: Resting state coherence measured with MEG is capa-
ble of mapping the functional connectivity of the brain, and can be
used for imaging damaged vs. intact tissue.

Introduction:Apallic Syndrome (AS) is a condition in which self-
awareness and awareness of environment is absent. Neuroimaging
studies suggest normal brain activity can be measured in AS. In
remission I–III according to Gerstenbrand patients exhibit deliber-
ate or cognitively mediated behaviour, consistently enough, for cli-
nicians to be able to distinguish it from reflexive responses. We
recently reported a selective response in the medial prefrontal cor-
tex (MPFC) to the subjects own name in a long-term AS patient. In
this study we examined brain activity in response to the subject’ s
own name in a larger sample of AS and in remission.
Methods: Brain activity was examined in 4 AS and 4 remissions
while hearing their own first name, compared with a different
name, using BOLD-fMRI. There were 7 controls.
Results: Higher activity for the own compared to another name in
the MPFC was found in the controls. This was only found in 1 AS
and 2 remissions. Additionally, 1 patient in remission exhibited a
selective response to his own name in the temporal cortex. Names
resulted in an activation of the auditory cortex in all subject’ s,
although with marked differences in strength and extent.
Discussion: Selective brain response to one’ s own name was found
in the controls and therefore seems to be a reliable paradigm to
examine residual language perception in disorders of conscious-
ness. In line with previous studies, there was evidence that in some
of the investigated patients the brain may still have some capacity
for language perception.

Objective: To investigate structure of muscle and cytoskeleton
proteins titin and nebulin in stiff person syndrome (SPS).
Background: A 49-year-old lady with stiffness and tension of
axial muscles developed vertical diplopia, dysarthrophonia, ataxia.
Brain MRI was normal. Global electromyography (EMG) showed
increased bioelectrical activity in axial muscles. Increase of anti-
bodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase was found. SPS was
diagnosed.
Design and methods:Biopsy from erector spinae muscle was ana-
lyzed using morphological and immuno-histochemical techniques;
titin, nebulin were investigated by gel-electrophoresis.
Results: Structure of the muscle tissue was normal. Analysis of
myosin heavy chains showed predominance of type I fibres. We
were first to investigate titin and nebulin in SPS: twofold decrease
was found.
Conclusions: Sustained increase of muscle activity leads to
destruction of titin and nebulin that result in impairment of sup-
porting/elastic properties of muscle sarcomere cytoskeleton, and to
reorganization of muscle tissue with slow fatigue resistant fibres
predominance.
